description:
memory.rs uses HashMap<(&'static str, String), V> for its three primary stores (objects at line 130, states at line 132, change_log at line 134). Every read calls .to_owned() on the &str account_id to construct the lookup key:

  fn current_state(&self, type_name: &'static str, account_id: &str) -> u64 {
      *self
          .states
          .get(&(type_name, account_id.to_owned()))   // <-- alloc on every read
          .unwrap_or(&0)
  }

This pattern fires on every JmapBackend read method (account_exists, get_objects, get_state, get_changes, query_objects, query_changes) — each call path eventually calls one of current_state(), objects_ref(), or change_log accessors and pays a String allocation per call. The (type_name, account_id.to_owned()) tuple is dropped immediately after lookup.

This is workspace-wide: the canonical jmap-mail-server has the same pattern at the same lines (memory.rs:137, :144, :157, :166, :213, etc.). Per workspace AGENTS.md, fix the canonical first, propagate to all 7 extension-server siblings.

Three idiomatic fixes available:
(a) Use a nested HashMap: HashMap<&'static str, HashMap<String, V>>. Lookups: self.objects.get(type_name).and_then(|m| m.get(account_id)). No tuple-key allocation. Costs one extra hash op per lookup but each hash is over a short &str.
(b) Use HashMap<(&'static str, &str), V> via a custom Borrow impl on a (&'static str, &str) wrapper. Stdlib doesn't give you Borrow<(&str, &str)> on (&str, String) tuples directly, so this needs a newtype.
(c) Cow<'static, str> for the second field, but you still pay allocation on the cold path.

Option (a) is the cleanest. It also makes the per-type indexing structure explicit (matching how the chat-server canonical describes 'multi-type-store' — see memory.rs:52-53).

This is a Rust-idiom concern (the .to_owned() at every key-read is unidiomatic for a hot path) and a minor performance concern (every state read does a heap allocation). For the reference impl's role as a 'documented example for backend implementors', the current shape teaches the wrong pattern.
title: MemoryBackend tuple-keyed HashMap allocates a String on every read
